questions.stem: What is the core idea of Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)?
options: Trust everyone inside the corporate network
No entity, human or machine, is trusted by default
Trust all devices that have antivirus installed
Trust users after a single login for life
questions.explanation: Zero Trust ensures that no entity, whether human or machine, is trusted by default, minimising the risk of unauthorised access.

questions.stem: Why is traditional perimeter-based security described as no longer sufficient?
options: Because security threats are more sophisticated and pervasive than ever
Because all data is now public
Because passwords are no longer used
Because networks are now entirely wireless
questions.explanation: In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, threats are more sophisticated and pervasive, so perimeter security cannot protect data on its own.

questions.stem: In Zero Trust Architecture, what is the starting baseline for access?
options: Devices on the intranet have access
questions.explanation: The architecture starts with a zero-trust baseline where no one has access, then gradually opens doors through verified credentials and monitoring.

questions.stem: Through which mechanisms are 'doors' slowly and carefully opened in a Zero Trust design?
questions.explanation: After the no-access baseline, doors are opened using Authentication, Authorisation and Entitlement approaches.

questions.stem: Which additional protections are applied even after access controls in Zero Trust Architecture?
options: Data or disk encryption, masking and anonymisation
questions.explanation: Even after access is granted, encryption, masking, anonymisation and other approaches ensure hackers and malware cannot get into the system.

questions.stem: Which of the following is named as opening doors for hackers and viruses in the current era?
options: Millions of IoT devices and thousands of mobile phones
questions.explanation: Hundreds of thousands of mobile phones, millions of IoT devices and on-prem versus cloud architectures all open doors for hackers and viruses.

questions.stem: What is described as THE most valuable asset in every organisation?
questions.explanation: Data has become the most valuable asset or critical element in every organisation, and compromising it can even lead to jail.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a benefit of implementing Zero Trust Architecture?
options: Significantly reduced risk of data breaches
Elimination of the need for encryption
questions.explanation: Zero Trust reduces breach risk, ensures compliance, streamlines operations and future-proofs security; encryption remains one of its layers, not something it removes.

questions.stem: Does 'no one' in Zero Trust refer only to human users?
options: Yes, it applies only to employees
Yes, it applies only to external contractors
It applies only to cloud accounts
No, it applies only to machines
No, it applies to humans and machines alike
questions.explanation: When Zero Trust says no one is trusted, it is not only about humans; it includes devices and machines as well.

questions.stem: How is the Zero Trust approach described in terms of how defences are maintained?
options: Outsourced entirely to the cloud provider
questions.explanation: Zero Trust is an adaptive approach that uses verified credentials and continuous monitoring so defences stay resilient against emerging threats.
